content: The Sweet Chestnut, scientifically known as Castanea sativa and belonging to the family Fagaceae, is also referred to as the Spanish Chestnut or European Chestnut. This species is native to southeastern Europe and Asia Minor. It is a deciduous tree that can grow to a height of 20 to 35 meters, with a trunk diameter often reaching up to 2 meters. The leaves are oblong-lanceolate in shape, with bold, toothed edges, measuring between 16 and 28 centimeters in length and 5 to 9 centimeters in width. The tree produces flowers of both sexes on upright catkins that are 10 to 20 centimeters long. The male flowers are located in the upper portion of the catkins, while the female flowers are found in the lower part. These flowers typically bloom from late June to July. By autumn, the female flowers develop into spiny cupules, each containing 3 to 7 brownish nuts, which are shed in October. This tree thrives in mild climates with sufficient moisture, which are essential for optimal growth and nut production. It is, however, sensitive to frost during late spring and early autumn and does not tolerate lime-rich soils. In forested environments, the Sweet Chestnut can adapt to moderate shade. The Sweet Chestnut is extensively cultivated for its edible nuts. Its cultivation dates back to Roman times, when it was introduced to more northern regions. Later, monks grew it in monastery gardens. Today, ancient specimens of the tree can be found in Great Britain as well as across central and western Europe. The nuts are widely used in confectionery and are commonly consumed roasted. They are particularly popular in countries such as Turkey, Portugal, France, Italy, and Corsica. The nuts can be roasted whole or ground into flour. In Corsica, a type of polenta known as pulenta is made using sweet chestnut flour, and a local variety of Corsican beer also incorporates chestnuts. Additionally, the fruit of the Japanese chestnut is edible. The wood of the Sweet Chestnut is durable and is used in the production of furniture, barrels (sometimes for aging balsamic vinegar), fencing, and roof beams, particularly in the Alpujarra region of Spain. However, due to its tendency to split and warp, it is not suitable for use in large pieces. The bark of the tree is also a source of tannin.
